evidence_set: As summarized: at about the end of the first week of abstinence from heroin, total sleep time, slow-wave, REM and stage 2 sleep were reduced and sleep latency, wake after sleep onset and REM latency increased compared with healthy sleepers (Howe et al.); during the first three weeks of abstinence, prolonged sleep latency, reduced efficiency and total sleep, more arousals and less slow-wave sleep compared with healthy sleepers (Asaad et al.); after six weeks to six months of abstinence from methadone, slow-wave and REM sleep rebounded above baseline.

As summarized: more than three-quarters of people in methadone maintenance report sleep complaints and about 50% report using both illicit drugs and legal medications to help with sleep; between 30 and 90% of patients on long-term opioid therapy show signs of central apnoea in a dose-dependent way; buprenorphine treatment in 70 patients with chronic opioid use was associated with mild to severe sleep-disordered breathing with a substantial rate of hypoxaemia.

evidence_set: As summarized: as alcohol use becomes chronic, alcohol has less of a hypnotic (sleep-promoting) effect; clinical insomnia in about 35 to 70% of alcohol users depending on the setting and stage of use, against about 15 to 30% in the general population; sleep complaints in alcohol use disorder are one of the most refractory problems to resolve, and insomnia is the most frequent complaint after stopping drinking.

As summarized: alcohol can shorten sleep latency in healthy people; in alcohol use disorder sleep latency is prolonged during drinking and acute and post-acute withdrawal, total sleep time is reduced, slow-wave sleep deficits may take months to years to recover, REM rebounds after stopping with inconsistent findings, and sleep-stage switches are increased compared with healthy controls from the second night of abstinence to as long as one to two years.

As summarized: self-reported insomnia during early abstinence predicted drinking or relapse in several studies; longer sleep latency in the first two weeks increased the odds of relapse in one study, longer sleep latency and lower sleep efficiency after 16 days and 19 weeks were associated with lower abstinence rates at 14 months in a second, and sleep latency at 5 days did not differ between later relapsers and abstainers in a third; slow-wave and REM measures gave mixed results.

evidence_set: As summarized: cannabis may improve subjective sleep in short-term use; with chronic use, withdrawal brings sleep difficulty, strange dreams, insomnia and poor sleep quality, in 32% to 76% of people experiencing withdrawal, in inpatient and outpatient studies and placebo-controlled discontinuation studies; strange dreams typically begin within days of stopping and can persist for weeks; returning to cannabis, alcohol or other sedatives to sleep is commonly observed; the sleep-promoting effect is lessened in chronic users compared with naive users.

As summarized: tolerance develops to the sleep-inducing and slow-wave effects with chronic use; polysomnography in withdrawal shows increased sleep onset latency and waking, reduced total sleep time, efficiency and slow-wave sleep, and REM rebound; changes can start as soon as the first night, are more noticeable in heavy use, progress over the first weeks and persist into abstinence.

evidence_set: As summarized: lofexidine plus oral THC gave the greatest benefit in one study, oral THC alone none; nabilone may reverse withdrawal-related sleep disruption; valproic acid gave no benefit and even some worsening of symptoms, and lithium, nefazodone and bupropion showed no definite benefit; zolpidem, mirtazapine, gabapentin and quetiapine improved sleep parameters but none conclusively reduced relapse.

evidence_set: One Dutch research programme recruited 81 participants in three equal groups (heavy GHB use with multiple GHB-induced comas; regular GHB use without comas; mild polydrug use, never GHB); the coma group performed worst on verbal memory, reported more anxiety, stress, depression and impulsivity, and showed differences in brain activity during memory and emotion tasks compared with the other two groups; the group with regular use without comas showed resting-state connectivity changes compared with the never-GHB group.

In 14 laboratory studies (8 to 49 participants each), GHB impaired digit-symbol, memory and psychomotor performance at moderate and higher doses, with modest or no effects at the lowest doses tested; memory impairment was less than with triazolam, pentobarbital or alcohol at the doses compared. The review classes all 14 as studies of acute effects, gives no test timings, and states it remains to be established whether the amnestic effects are reversible.

evidence_set: 48 studies (52 publications), 1774 participants: 16 psilocybin, 16 ayahuasca, 10 LSD, 2 5-MeO-DMT, 3 several, 1 mescaline; sample sizes 6 to 315 (median 18). 14 studies (29%) had a standardized treatment, placebo control and double-blind allocation; 19 (40%) a standardized treatment but no control group and/or no double-blind allocation; 15 (31%) no standardized treatment (e.g. observational studies).

Changes were observed most consistently (in 70 to 90% of studies investigating the domain, more than 450 participants each) for depression, stress and grief; mindfulness, acceptance and emotion regulation; personality, values and attitudes; wellbeing; and social effects. At group level no worsening of psychopathology was reported, and there was no evidence of increases in suicidality, manic or psychotic symptoms or of decreases in cognitive performance, though few studies assessed these.

evidence_set: Flashbacks were unpleasant for 2 (1.4% of all 142) and neutral or positive for 10; one case was not sufficiently documented. No one reported impairment of daily life. One distressing case followed an exceptionally difficult session and the participant left the study; the other was a single episode during escitalopram pretreatment after psilocybin, followed by panic attacks, after which the participant left the study.

One participant had about 30 brief, benign visual flashbacks over seven months, which had stopped about ten months before follow-up; at follow-up (mean 31.2 months later, 12 of 13 responding, one incompletely) she was the only one who clearly reported recurrence after the end-of-study visit.

Exclusions included current or previous psychotic or major psychiatric disorder, psychotic disorder in a first-degree relative, and more than ten prior illicit drug uses (cannabis excepted). Three of the 13 had also received escitalopram, d-amphetamine or MDMA. The authors list the sample size, varied doses and substances, likely positive attitudes, follow-up only of those with flashbacks, and exclusion of people with mental disorders as limitations.
